beats.narration_text: Salaam. This is Liam, in for Bear, with a short film for INFO seventy-three seventy-five, Computational Skepticism for AI. You might think a good skeptic doubts everything. You can't, and you shouldn't try. The real question is what to doubt.

show.event: backspaces 'everything' -> 'what my work depends on' on the spoken correction

beats.motion_claim: The writer types the naive question (should I doubt everything) and corrects it to the real one (should I doubt what my work depends on).

qc.sparse_reason: Hesitant-writer bookend: the correction is the motion.

beats.narration_text: Three terms. Radical doubt: asking what would have to be true for a claim to be wrong. Risk: how likely a claim is to be wrong, and what it costs if it is. And a provisional code: rules you act by while you're still doubting.

terms.meaning: asking what would make a claim wrong
how likely it's wrong, and what that costs
rules to act by while you doubt

qc.sparse_reason: TERMS card: three prerequisites, one line each.

beats.narration_text: In his Meditations, published in sixteen forty-one, Day-cart set out, once in his life, to tear down every belief he could find any reason to doubt, and rebuild from the foundations. He says it was safe to go that far because he was after knowledge, not action.

shot.visual_intent: A wall of kraft belief blocks on a dark foundation ('beliefs'); the labels 'Descartes' and 'Meditations, 1641'; cracks appear on every block but one and the cracked blocks lift away, leaving the foundation and one block, which gets a terracotta dot on 'knowledge, not action'.

show.event: cracked blocks lift away: tear down

shot.motion_claim: A wall of kraft belief blocks on a dark foundation ('beliefs'); the labels 'Descartes' and 'Meditations, 1641'; cracks appear on every block but one and the cracked blocks lift away, leaving the foundation and one block, which gets a terracotta dot on 'knowledge, not action'.

beats.narration_text: This course borrows his move as one question you can ask of any claim: what would have to be true for this to be wrong? The answer isn't a mood. It's a list of things you can go and check.

shot.visual_intent: A white claim card on a kraft stand ('claim'); an ink magnifier, the doubt lens, slides over it ('doubt'); a clipboard lands beside it and three rows tick one by one ('checklist').

show.event: the lens: what would make it wrong
three rows tick: a list you can check

shot.motion_claim: A white claim card on a kraft stand ('claim'); an ink magnifier, the doubt lens, slides over it ('doubt'); a clipboard lands beside it and three rows tick one by one ('checklist').

beats.narration_text: But you can't run that question on everything. Every check costs time. Doubt every claim you meet, and you never get to act, and the work just waits.

shot.visual_intent: A long row of claim cards ('claims'); the lens checks them one at a time, a check over each, while an hourglass drains ('time'); four more cards arrive at the back of the row faster than the lens can check them.

show.event: the lens checks one at a time; the hourglass drains
more keep arriving: the work waits

shot.motion_claim: A long row of claim cards ('claims'); the lens checks them one at a time, a check over each, while an hourglass drains ('time'); four more cards arrive at the back of the row faster than the lens can check them.

beats.narration_text: Day-cart saw this. In his Discourse on the Method, from sixteen thirty-seven, he says that while you pull down your house to rebuild it, you need another house to live in. So while he doubted, he kept a provisional code: a few rules to act by.

shot.visual_intent: The belief house from B00 under rebuilding at the left ('rebuilding'); a small kraft cabin drops in at the right, its window lights ('Discourse, 1637'); three rule pages slide in beside the cabin ('provisional code').

show.event: a few rules to act by

shot.motion_claim: The belief house from B00 under rebuilding at the left ('rebuilding'); a small kraft cabin drops in at the right, its window lights ('Discourse, 1637'); three rule pages slide in beside the cabin ('provisional code').

beats.narration_text: One rule: a traveler lost in a forest shouldn't wander from side to side, or stand still. Pick a direction and walk straight, and you'll likely end up somewhere better than the middle of the forest. When you can't tell what's true and you have to act, act on what's most probable.

shot.visual_intent: An isometric forest of kraft trees with an ink traveller peg in the middle ('lost'); a grey wandering path scribbles and fades; then a straight ink path draws out to the forest edge and the peg walks it to a terracotta dot ('straight on').
shot.motion_claim: An isometric forest of kraft trees with an ink traveller peg in the middle ('lost'); a grey wandering path scribbles and fades; then a straight ink path draws out to the forest edge and the peg walks it to a terracotta dot ('straight on').

beats.narration_text: So aim the doubt. Ask two things about a claim: how likely is it to be wrong, and what would it cost if it were? Together, that's risk. Treat this as a way of thinking, not a measured model.

shot.visual_intent: A 3 x 3 isometric floor on a dark plinth; grey axis arrows grow along one edge ('chance wrong') and the other ('cost if wrong'); on 'that's risk' the tiles shade darker toward high chance x high cost; a small label 'not measured'.
shot.motion_claim: A 3 x 3 isometric floor on a dark plinth; grey axis arrows grow along one edge ('chance wrong') and the other ('cost if wrong'); on 'that's risk' the tiles shade darker toward high chance x high cost; a small label 'not measured'.

beats.narration_text: The chair you're sitting on has held you for years, and if it failed, you'd land on the floor. Don't doubt it. Sit down. Most claims in a working day live in this corner: act on them, and fix them if they break.

shot.visual_intent: A kraft chair drops onto the low-chance, low-cost corner tile ('chair'); then small kraft claim blocks drop onto the other low tiles ('just act').

beats.narration_text: A few claims land over here: a triage score on a patient, a medication dose, the number your job depends on. If one of those is wrong, someone pays for it. Those get the doubt.

shot.visual_intent: On the high-cost row, three tall dark towers rise one after another ('triage score', 'dose', 'your number'); the doubt lens swings over them ('doubt hard').

show.event: triage score, dose, your number rise

shot.motion_claim: On the high-cost row, three tall dark towers rise one after another ('triage score', 'dose', 'your number'); the doubt lens swings over them ('doubt hard').

beats.narration_text: The rule is proportion. The more it costs to be wrong, the more doubt a claim gets. Cheap to be wrong: act, and watch. Costly to be wrong: stop, and ask what would have to be true for it to be wrong, before the world answers for you.

shot.visual_intent: A balance on a grey post: a small kraft cost block on the left pan, one doubt weight on the right, level ('cost if wrong', 'doubt'); the cost block is replaced by a tall dark one and the beam tips; three doubt weights drop onto the right pan and it levels again; the lens comes to the costly block.

show.event: small cost, a little doubt: level

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Write down five claims your work relied on this week, and paste this into Claude: Here are five claims my work relied on this week: paste them. For each one, help me say what it would cost if it were wrong, and rank them by that cost. Then, for the top one or two only, ask: what would have to be true for this to be wrong? List conditions I can check. Then check two things yourself. Are the top two really the ones that could hurt someone? And could you test each condition this week?
